item.content:encoded:
In some universe out there, Nick Offerman has a son, and he's a nasty left-handed pitcher for the Boston Red Sox. At least, that's how Offerman sees it.
The Chicago Cubs fan, actor and comedian who plays Ron Swanson (Parks and Rec) appeared on "The Joy of Baseball" podcast. He praised Payton Tolle for the skills and fun he brings to the game, and also took full credit for the mustache, joking that he could be his father. Tolle fired back with "Come to my arms papa," on social media which might be the most exciting Red Sox news of the offseason, so far.
If you hadn't noticed the resemblance before now, I'm sorry for pointing it out, because you won't be able to unsee it. When you put the two side by side you really need a DNA test to tell them and the mustaches apart.
I visited High-A Greenville last year, and Drive general manager Eric Jarinko told me he was the most impressive pitcher he'd ever seen, and one of the coolest, most down-to-earth guys, too.
Tolle is doing his part to fit in with the Red Sox, not just on the field but in Red Sox facial hair history, as well. Facial hair has always been part of the Red Sox identity, so we found the most iconic mustaches ever worn in a Sox uniform. We mostly stuck to household names and ranked them on accolades, history and a few personal connections. If you want to go down the rabbit hole yourself, this isn't the first time BoSox Injection has shown love to Red Sox mustaches — we covered the subject back in 2014, and for Sox fans this list gets really in the weeds, enjoy.
10 of the most iconic mustaches in Red Sox history as Payton Tolle keeps the tradition going
Luis Tiant
El Tiante gets the top spot because he wore No. 23, the number I was going to wear before I was traded from the Red Sox (I even had to ask for his blessing) and he was still rocking the stache then. The handlebar went with a one-of-a-kind windup, and he won 20 or more games three times in Boston.
Payton Tolle
The personality, the parted pencil mustache Over the Monster called "a statement," and the electric stuff are why he ranks this high. He went 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts this year, and is officially endorsed by Offerman.
Dwight Evans
"Dewey" played in Boston from 1972 to 1990 and grew the mustache in the '80s as he became one of the AL's top hitters. He later served as a special advisor to the general manager and was always around spring training when I was there, a super nice, soft-spoken guy.
Wade Boggs
I grew up a Yankee fan, so I remember him clean-shaven in pinstripes. But I always heard how historic he was in Boston, along with the reputation: allegedly 64 beers on a flight, and fried chicken before every game.
Jerry Remy
RemDawg's mustache followed him from second base to the NESN booth, and he was part of the NESN crew. He's got to get some love.
Dennis Eckersley
He went 20-8 with a 2.99 ERA in his first Boston season, then reinvented himself as an electric closer on his way to Cooperstown. He also broadcast for NESN and is deeply missed in the booth.
Jim Rice
Rice hit 382 homers, won the 1978 AL MVP, and kept the mustache through all of it.
Alex Bregman
His Tom Selleck-style mustache lasted until June 6, 2025, when he shaved it between innings against the Yankees to spark a rally. It didn't work, but it's an iconic moment in modern Red Sox pop culture.
Garrett Richards
He started his in 2020 when the pandemic shut down camp, and he told WEEI, "My wife absolutely hates it, bless her heart." A Boston radio show challenged him to curl the ends up Rollie Fingers-style.
Bill Buckner
This is not a slight, because most Red Sox fans have a sour taste in their mouths, but he shouldn't be reduced to one grounder. He had 2,715 hits and a 1980 batting title, and the mustache deserves better than a footnote.
Honorable mentions go to Rod Beck's fu manchu, Tony Armas' afro-and-mustache combo and Jody Reed, whose lip helped start that 2014 list in the first place.
The 2013 beard era took over Boston's upper lip for a while, but mustaches are creeping back, and Tolle has one of the best in baseball right now. This franchise has never been short on characters, from Tiant's windup to Bregman's mid-game shave. Pedro Martinez called Tolle "a bully," and he fits right in. If he keeps this up, he could be a face of this franchise for years, and the mustache will be right there with him.

item.content:encoded:
On the edge of the wind-scoured Salt Lake Valley, between rows of gray and white houses and sunbaked driveways, you can find a little taste of Fenway Park.
A housing subdivision in Herriman, Utah, is turning heads online for its streets, each of which bears the name of a Red Sox star from the annals of team history: Pesky Lane, Pedroia Street, and Varitek Drive, to name a few.
The names, which could be ripped straight from the banners on Van Ness Street, stand out in a place like Herriman, a Salt Lake City suburb 500 miles from the nearest Major League Baseball stadium. There’s little else to suggest Copper Fields, a neat grid of roughly 200 houses completed by Edge Homes in 2024, has a link to Boston.
But once social media caught wind of the Sox-heavy ‘hood over the weekend, fans were ablaze with speculation.
“Ready to blow my savings and move to Utah so I can live on Pedroia Street,” one commenter wrote on X, posting an image of a three-bed, three-bath home on sale for $669,000 (slightly cheaper than a 700-square-foot condo in the South End).
“[I don’t care] about getting priced out of Boston,” opined Anna Caruso of Section 10, a Red Sox podcast, beneath a photo of the development. “You’ll find me here.”
Another commenter said that, in person, the neighborhood is “brand-new and pretty nice,” though “all of the houses look basically the same.”
“I wonder what [percentage] of families that live here have no idea what the streets mean,” they added.
So, who’s behind all these names? There’s not much of a Red Sox connection in the area to speak of, aside from the fact that a young David Ortiz played with Salt Lake’s minor league team while still a Minnesota Twins prospect.
But that didn’t matter to Brandon Parr, the Edge Homes project manager who selected the names. Parr, 47, was born and raised in Utah — but he lives and breathes the Red Sox all the same.
“I liked Wade Boggs a lot, and he just happened to play for them, so I became a fan,” he said. “The rest is history.”
When Parr got the chance to name an entire new subdivision, his vision was clear.
“I don’t think anybody on my team really knew what I was doing until they saw the first flat be recorded [on the master plan],” he said.
Parr made sure to include a (Wade) Boggs Way, as well as a (Jerry) Remy Road, named after the late broadcaster and former player, and a Xander (Bogaerts) Lane. The neighborhood even has a Yawkey Way, named after the controversial Red Sox owner whose name once marked what is now Jersey Street. (Edge Homes seems to have missed the memo on that one.)
Plenty of fans online wondered why Parr didn’t nod toward other Red Sox legends. The answer, he said, was that some names were hard to get local approval for. Ted Williams, for example, had a surname common enough that there’s already a Camp Williams Road in town.
“Some of them are personal favorites,” Parr said of the player names. “I was a big fan of Nathan Eovaldi and his performance in 2018, so he’s on there. ... Boggs was the reason I started liking the Red Sox, so I had to get him. I was just trying to pick some names that meant something to me, and to the organization as well.”
It’s not the first time Parr has gotten creative with street names. Edge Homes takes on anywhere from 10 to 12 development projects a year, and naming all those streets can be “a little bit of a daunting task sometimes,” he said.
Aside from Red Sox players, Parr has also referenced comic book movie actors. A subdivision in Riverton, Utah, includes a Hemsworth Lane and a Hiddleston Drive, named after Chris Hemsworth and Tom Hiddleston, the actors who play Thor and Loki in Marvel films.
“My company encourages us to be creative,” he said. “It’s just something fun that we do as a team.”
Parr, who carries a Red Sox water bottle and owns a replica championship ring, has taken his family to a few games at Fenway. But he admits that Red Sox fans aren’t exactly plentiful in Salt Lake City.
“I’m kind of alone,” he said. “At the office, I would say there’s definitely more Yankees fans around me than Red Sox fans. But I’ll be a Red Sox fan till the day I die.”
At least one Herriman resident recognizes the significance of the street names.
Chris Watson, 56, a graphic designer and photographer, has lived in Utah for over two decades. But he was raised in Framingham, collecting Red Sox trading cards and watching Luis Tiant and Jim Rice and Carl Yastrzemski.
“I don’t keep up with [the team] as much anymore,” he said. “But the only baseball hat I’ll wear is a Red Sox hat.”
When he was searching for a place to build a new home a few years back, he realized “really quickly” the names on the lot were something special.
It was a “really fun coincidence” to end up living on Fisk Road — named after Carlton Fisk, Watson’s favorite player on the (in)famous 1978 team. Even that team, lamented for its end-of-season collapse against the Yankees, still holds a special place in his heart.
“That was the peak of fandom for my 8, 9-year old self,” he said. “He would have thought it was really cool [to be living here].”

Andrew Bailey, Craig Breslow, and Kurt Suzuki were teammates with the Oakland Athletics from 2009-11. Now Bailey is the Red Sox pitching coach, Breslow is chief baseball officer, and Suzuki is managing the Angels.
Suzuki, a former catcher, knows the Red Sox pitching coach and chief baseball officer well. Bailey was a two-time All-Star closer with the Athletics, and Breslow made 202 appearances as a setup man during that time.
“I thought Bres would cure cancer when he was finished with baseball,” said Suzuki, referencing the lefthander graduating from Yale with a degree in molecular biophysics and biochemistry. “But I can see why he stayed in baseball. He was always ahead of the times the way he thought about the game.
“When I caught him, I called him ‘Everyday Bres.’ He was always ready to pitch every day, never complained, and always got people out. He was a good person to be around.”
Suzuki is not surprised to see his former teammates still involved in the game.
“I think we all love the game. We all had an interest to stay in the game beyond our playing time,” he said. “Bres pitched in the big leagues for a long time and gained a lot of information. I don’t know if I would have predicted he’d be running a team, but I’m not surprised.
“The same with [Bailey]. You knew he would have a bright future in the game if that was what he wanted. He’s one of the best pitching coaches around.”
A few other observations on the Red Sox:
▪ It seems funny to think about now, but Aroldis Chapman came to spring training in 2025 with no guarantee he would be the closer.
The lefthander was competing with Liam Hendriks, who was returning from Tommy John surgery. Breslow said at the time Justin Slaten also would receive consideration.
Chapman had 14 saves for the Pirates in 2024, but nine of them came in September for a last-place team.
Hendriks never had a save for the Sox. Slaten had one in March and two in April that season, and none since.
Chapman has converted 65 of 69 save opportunities for the Sox and taken steps that could lead to the Hall of Fame.
▪ No Red Sox infielder has won a Gold Glove since Ian Kinsler in 2018, and he joined the team at the trade deadline that season and started only 35 games at second base. For a full season, you have to go back to Pedroia in 2014.
Caleb Durbin is set to break that drought.
The third baseman has 11 defensive runs saved, the most in the American League by a wide margin. Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero, with three, is a distant second. Durbin also leads in other metrics, including outs above average.
▪ As the season winds down, Wilyer Abreu is first in doubles, second in runs and home runs, fourth in RBIs, and fifth in OPS among AL outfielders.
The right fielder believes playing in the World Baseball Classic contributed significantly to that success.
“I worked a lot in the offseason to be prepared for the WBC,” Abreu said. “So when the season started, I was ready to go. That helped me a lot.”
Abreu also benefited from being around Venezuela hitting coach Miguel Cabrera and assistant manager Victor Martinez.
“I talked a lot to them about my approach and how to attack pitchers on what they throw,” he said. “Miggy was such a smart hitter, and he really helped me.”
▪ Fred Lynn was at Fenway Park for the Angels series this past week. He follows the Sox closely and often arrives at the park early to watch batting practice.
Most of the players had no idea who the 74-year-old guy with the good tan was, but Roman Anthony did and had a conversation on the field with Lynn on Tuesday.
“He was somebody I’d wanted to meet for a while, obviously. A legend,” Anthony said. “Somebody said he was out there, so I immediately wanted to say hello to him and his wife, and they were great.
“He shared some of his experiences here, his experiences when he left here. It was great to hear it.”
No. 19 talking to No. 19 was interesting to watch from a distance. Anthony received a lot of attention when he was called up last year, but nothing like the mania for Lynn and Jim Rice in 1975.
Anthony has looked up the statistics. He gets it.
“I got familiar with him when I got 19 when I first came up last year,” he said. “He was pretty excited about it and sent some love. Obviously, he was an unbelievable player, an unbelievable Red Sox. But a great human, too. It was awesome to interact with him.”
▪ The Sox traded for Curtis Mead on July 26. He started at second base against the Athletics in Sacramento the next day, and broke his left wrist when he was hit by a pitch in his second plate appearance.
Red Sox second basemen have since hit .245 with a .718 OPS and 21 RBIs. It’s not great, but nine American League teams have a lower OPS from their second basemen in that span, and 10 have a lower wRC+.
As for Mead, he is playing catch but isn’t hitting yet. The Sox haven’t ruled him out for the rest of the season, but interim manager Chad Tracy has acknowledged it’s unlikely Mead will return until 2027.
Connelly Early, who was traded for Mead, has yet to pitch for the Nationals because of an elbow injury. He is scheduled to make a rehab start for Double-A Harrisburg on Sunday. The Nationals hope he’ll be able to get into a major league game before the season ends.
▪ Baseball lost a legend last week when Joe McDonald passed away at the age of 97.
McDonald started in baseball in the 1940s working with the ticket takers at Ebbets Field. He joined the Mets in 1962 and became their general manager from 1975-80.
He later became GM of the Cardinals (1982-84) and Tigers (1991-92) before scouting for the Angels and Rockies. He finished his career scouting for the Red Sox from 2004-19.
“Joe was a joy to work with and always very generous in sharing his experience and expertise. He loved the game, was willing to go scout a player anywhere at any time, and just wanted to contribute,” said former Sox GM and current Fenway Sports Group senior adviser Theo Epstein, who hired McDonald. “Having two great former GMs like Joe and Bill Lajoie around was incredibly valuable to me. He will be missed.”
